tiles.title: Type Conversion and Datetime Handling
tiles.summary: Learn to convert column dtypes with astype and to work with datetime data using pd.to_datetime and the .dt accessor.

steps.title: Fixing column types with astype
steps.lede: When a CSV loads numbers as text, arithmetic fails. astype() converts a column to the right dtype in one call.

blocks.text: Suppose the SwiftDrop export loads `distance_km` as text — values like `"12.5"` instead of actual floats. Until the dtype is fixed, pandas treats the column as strings and arithmetic on it will fail.

The `astype()` method explicitly converts a column's values from one dtype to another, returning a copy by default. It raises an exception if the conversion is invalid — so `orders["distance_km"].astype(float)` converts text values to floats, but a row containing `"unknown"` would raise an error rather than silently guessing.
`astype()` can convert multiple columns at once by passing a dict: `orders.astype({"distance_km": float, "order_id": str})` converts two columns to two different target types in a single call.

before.code:
# distance_km loaded as object (text)
print(orders["distance_km"].dtype)  # object
print(orders["distance_km"].head())  # '4.2', '6.1', '5.5' ...

annotations.text: dtype is 'object' — pandas stores these as strings
Values look numeric but are text; arithmetic would fail

after.code:
orders["distance_km"] = orders["distance_km"].astype(float)
print(orders["distance_km"].dtype)  # float64
# Now arithmetic works: orders["distance_km"].mean()

annotations.text: astype(float) converts every text value to a real float
dtype is now float64 — arithmetic is possible

blocks.change_summary: distance_km column converted from object (text) to float64 using astype(float).

steps.title: Turning date text into real datetimes
steps.lede: A pickup_date column stored as text can't answer date questions. pd.to_datetime converts it, and .dt unlocks its components.

blocks.text: Suppose the SwiftDrop export records each order's `pickup_date` as plain text — `"2024-03-14"`. Before you can ask which month had the most deliveries, that text needs to become an actual datetime value.

`pd.to_datetime()` converts a Series of date-like strings into pandas datetime values, returning a Series with the same index: `orders["pickup_date"] = pd.to_datetime(orders["pickup_date"])` replaces the text column with genuine datetime values, one per order, in the same row positions.

Once a column has a datetime dtype, its `.dt` accessor exposes date component properties for each value: `orders["pickup_month"] = orders["pickup_date"].dt.month` pulls just the month number out of every pickup date at once.

before.code:
# pickup_date is object dtype (text)
print(orders["pickup_date"].dtype)   # object
print(orders["pickup_date"].head())  # '2024-03-14', '2024-03-14', '2024-03-15', ...

annotations.text: dtype is 'object' — dates stored as plain strings
Values look like dates but pandas can't do date arithmetic yet

after.code:
orders["pickup_date"] = pd.to_datetime(orders["pickup_date"])
orders["pickup_month"] = orders["pickup_date"].dt.month
print(orders["pickup_date"].dtype)   # datetime64[ns]
print(orders[["pickup_date", "pickup_month"]].head())

annotations.text: to_datetime converts text strings to real datetime values
.dt.month extracts the month number from each datetime
dtype is now datetime64[ns]

blocks.change_summary: pickup_date converted from object to datetime64 with pd.to_datetime; a new pickup_month column extracted via .dt.month.

steps.title: Type conversion and datetime handling — key takeaways
steps.lede: Two tools for fixing column types: astype for general conversions, to_datetime for dates.

blocks.text: `astype()` is the general-purpose dtype converter — pass a target type for one column or a dict for several at once. It raises an exception on invalid conversions rather than guessing. For date columns, `pd.to_datetime()` is the one-time conversion step; after that, `.dt` unlocks pulling out whatever date component the analysis needs.

blocks.title: Up next: Text Cleaning, Duplicates, and Missing Data
blocks.text: Next you'll clean messy text columns with the .str accessor, remove duplicate rows, and handle missing values — the three most common data-quality fixes after dtype correction.

remediation_steps.title: Converting multiple columns with a dict
remediation_steps.lede: astype accepts a dict so you can convert several columns to different types in one call.

blocks.text: `astype()` can convert a single column or multiple columns at once. Pass a dict mapping column names to target dtypes: `orders.astype({"distance_km": float, "order_id": str})` converts `distance_km` to float and `order_id` to string in one call — no need to call astype twice.

before.code:
# Two separate astype calls — works but verbose
orders["distance_km"] = orders["distance_km"].astype(float)
orders["order_id"] = orders["order_id"].astype(str)

annotations.text: Two separate calls — one per column

after.code:
# One astype call with a dict — converts both columns at once
orders = orders.astype({"distance_km": float, "order_id": str})

annotations.text: Dict maps each column name to its target dtype

blocks.change_summary: Two separate astype calls replaced by one dict-based call.

remediation_steps.title: Extracting date components with .dt
remediation_steps.lede: After converting a column to datetime, the .dt accessor exposes year, month, day, and more for every row at once.

blocks.text: Once a column has a datetime dtype, its `.dt` accessor exposes date/time component properties — such as `year`, `month`, and `day` — for each value: `orders["pickup_month"] = orders["pickup_date"].dt.month` pulls just the month number out of every pickup date at once. Without the `.dt` accessor, you cannot access these properties on a datetime Series.

before.code:
# pickup_date is still text — .dt is not available
# orders["pickup_date"].dt.month  # AttributeError

annotations.text: Text column has no .dt accessor — must convert first

after.code:
orders["pickup_date"] = pd.to_datetime(orders["pickup_date"])
orders["pickup_month"] = orders["pickup_date"].dt.month
orders["pickup_day"]   = orders["pickup_date"].dt.day

annotations.text: Convert once with to_datetime
.dt.month and .dt.day each extract one component for every row

blocks.change_summary: pickup_date converted to datetime; month and day extracted via .dt accessor.

tiles.title: Text Cleaning, Duplicates, and Missing Data
tiles.summary: Clean text columns with the .str accessor, remove duplicate rows with drop_duplicates, and handle missing values with isna, dropna, and fillna.

steps.title: Cleaning a text column with the .str accessor
steps.lede: Mixed-case and padded city names cause mismatches. The .str accessor applies string methods across an entire column at once.

blocks.text: Suppose the `city` column in a SwiftDrop export has `"Lagos"`, `" lagos"`, and `"LAGOS "` scattered across different rows — the same city, written three inconsistent ways. Grouping or filtering by city will miss rows until the values are standardised.

A Series' `.str` accessor lets you call ordinary string-processing methods — matching the names of Python's built-in string methods such as `lower`, `strip`, and `replace` — on every element of the Series at once: `orders["city"].str.strip().str.lower()` removes stray whitespace and lowercases every city value in one chained call, turning all three variants into the same `"lagos"`.

before.caption: city column before cleaning — mixed case and stray spaces

annotations.text: .str.strip() removes leading/trailing spaces; .str.lower() lowercases every value
All three variants now collapse to the same lowercase form

blocks.change_summary: city column cleaned: stray whitespace stripped and all values lowercased in one chained .str call.

steps.title: Lowercasing every value in a column at once
steps.lede: Watch a single .str.lower() call change every row in a column.

steps.title: Removing duplicate rows with drop_duplicates
steps.lede: A repeated order_id means the same order was logged twice. drop_duplicates removes the extra row, keeping the occurrence you choose.

blocks.text: Suppose order `#1003` appears twice in the SwiftDrop orders DataFrame, logged the same way both times. Any count or aggregation will be inflated until the duplicate is removed.

`duplicated()` returns a boolean vector indicating which rows are duplicates, and `drop_duplicates()` removes them; both accept a `subset` argument naming the columns used to identify a duplicated row: `orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])` removes rows that repeat the same `order_id`.

By default, `drop_duplicates()` keeps the first occurrence of each duplicate set and drops the rest. Passing `keep='last'` keeps the last occurrence instead; `keep=False` drops every row that is part of a duplicate set: `orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"], keep="last")` would keep order `#1003`'s second logged row instead of its first.

before.caption: orders before deduplication — order_id 1003 appears twice

after.code:
orders_clean = orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])
print(len(orders_clean))  # one row per order_id

annotations.text: subset=["order_id"] means two rows with the same order_id count as duplicates
Result has one row per unique order_id; first occurrence kept by default

blocks.change_summary: Duplicate order rows removed by drop_duplicates(subset=['order_id']); first occurrence kept.

steps.title: Detecting, dropping, and filling missing values
steps.lede: Blank cells in a DataFrame are missing values. isna detects them; dropna removes affected rows; fillna replaces them.

blocks.text: Suppose a handful of SwiftDrop orders never got a `delivery_time_minutes` recorded — those cells are just blank. Any mean or sum on that column will be wrong unless the gaps are handled first.
`isna()` (and its complement `notna()`) detects which values in a Series or DataFrame are missing: `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].isna()` returns `True` for every order missing that value.

`dropna()` removes rows that contain missing values; passing a `subset` of column labels restricts which columns are checked: `orders.dropna(subset=["delivery_time_minutes"])` removes only the orders missing that one column, ignoring gaps elsewhere.

`fillna()` replaces missing values with a specified value: `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].fillna(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median())` replaces each missing delivery time with the column's median instead of dropping the order entirely.

before.caption: orders before handling missing values — some delivery_time_minutes are blank

after.code:
# Option A: drop rows missing delivery_time_minutes
orders_dropped = orders.dropna(subset=["delivery_time_minutes"])

# Option B: fill missing values with the column median
median_time = orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median()
orders["delivery_time_minutes"] = orders["delivery_time_minutes"].fillna(median_time)

annotations.text: dropna with subset removes only rows missing this column
fillna replaces each blank with the column's median value

blocks.change_summary: Missing delivery_time_minutes handled: either dropped with dropna(subset=...) or filled with the column median via fillna.

steps.title: Text cleaning, duplicates, and missing data — key takeaways
steps.lede: Three essential data-quality tools: .str for text, drop_duplicates for repeated rows, and isna/dropna/fillna for gaps.

blocks.text: Whatever string method you'd call on one piece of text, the `.str` accessor applies across an entire column at once. `drop_duplicates(subset=[...])` removes repeated rows by key column, keeping the first occurrence by default. Handling missing data means detecting it first with `isna()`, then deciding: drop the row if the missing field makes it unusable, or fill with a reasonable substitute such as the column's median.

blocks.title: Up next: Mapping and Applying Transformations
blocks.text: Next you'll use map substitution to replace values in a column using a lookup dict — a fast way to recode categories without writing loops.

remediation_steps.title: The .str accessor applies string methods to every row
remediation_steps.lede: Instead of looping row by row, the .str accessor vectorises any Python string method across the whole column.

blocks.text: A Series' `.str` accessor lets you call ordinary string-processing methods — matching the names of Python's built-in string methods such as `lower`, `strip`, and `replace` — on every element of the Series at once. `orders["city"].str.strip().str.lower()` removes stray whitespace and lowercases every city value in one chained call, turning `"Lagos"`, `" lagos"`, and `"LAGOS "` all into `"lagos"`.

annotations.text: Row-by-row loop — slow and verbose

after.code:
# With .str — one vectorised call
orders["city"] = orders["city"].str.strip().str.lower()

annotations.text: .str applies strip and lower to every element at once

blocks.change_summary: Row-by-row loop replaced by a single chained .str.strip().str.lower() call.

remediation_steps.title: Using subset to identify duplicate rows
remediation_steps.lede: drop_duplicates checks all columns by default. The subset argument limits the check to the columns that define a duplicate.

blocks.text: `duplicated()` returns a boolean vector indicating which rows are duplicates, and `drop_duplicates()` removes them; both accept a `subset` argument naming the columns used to identify a duplicated row. `orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])` removes rows that repeat the same `order_id`, even if other columns differ slightly between the two rows.

before.code:
# Without subset — checks ALL columns; rows must be identical
orders.drop_duplicates()

annotations.text: Only removes rows where every column matches — misses partial duplicates
Removes any row whose order_id already appeared — correct for this case

blocks.change_summary: drop_duplicates called with subset=['order_id'] to catch rows with the same order ID regardless of other column differences.

remediation_steps.title: Drop or fill — choosing the right approach
remediation_steps.lede: dropna removes rows with missing values; fillna replaces them. The right choice depends on whether a reasonable substitute exists.

blocks.text: `dropna()` removes rows that contain missing values; passing a `subset` of column labels restricts which columns are checked. `fillna()` replaces missing values with a specified value. Drop the row if a missing field makes it unusable for the analysis; fill it if a reasonable substitute — such as the column's median — exists instead.

before.code:
# Missing delivery_time_minutes — two options
print(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].isna().sum())  # count of missing

annotations.text: isna().sum() counts how many values are missing

after.code:
# Drop rows where delivery_time_minutes is missing
orders_dropped = orders.dropna(subset=["delivery_time_minutes"])

# OR fill missing values with the column median
orders["delivery_time_minutes"] = orders["delivery_time_minutes"].fillna(
    orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median()
)

annotations.text: dropna removes rows missing this column
fillna replaces each blank with the median — no rows lost

blocks.change_summary: Missing delivery_time_minutes handled with either dropna (removes rows) or fillna with median (preserves rows).

tiles.title: Descriptive Statistics with pandas
tiles.summary: Compute mean, median, and standard deviation for a DataFrame column, and use describe() to get a full summary in one call.

steps.title: Computing statistics directly from a column
steps.lede: pandas can compute the mean, median, and standard deviation you've calculated by hand — straight from a DataFrame column.

blocks.text: The mean, median, and standard deviation computed by hand earlier for the seven-value delivery-time batch are exactly what pandas can compute directly from a DataFrame column.

pandas provides built-in statistical methods for a Series or DataFrame column, including `mean()` (mean of values), `median()` (arithmetic median), and `std()` (sample standard deviation): if `delivery_time_minutes` holds that seven-order batch, `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].mean()`, `.median()`, and `.std()` reproduce the same approximately 30.9, 22, and 21.9-minute figures straight from the column.

`describe()` computes a set of summary statistics — count, mean, std, min, quartiles, and max — for a Series or for each numeric column of a DataFrame in one call: `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].describe()` returns all of those figures at once for the delivery-time column.

annotations.text: describe() returns count, mean, std, min, quartiles, and max in one call

steps.title: Descriptive statistics with pandas — key takeaways
steps.lede: mean, median, std, and describe give you a complete picture of a numeric column in seconds.

blocks.text: pandas provides `mean()`, `median()`, and `std()` as direct methods on a Series or column. `describe()` bundles count, mean, std, min, quartiles, and max into one call. For the SwiftDrop delivery-time column, the mean (~30.9 min) sits well above the median (22 min) because a single 80-minute outlier pulls the average up — a pattern describe() makes immediately visible.

blocks.title: Up next: Selecting and Filtering Data
blocks.text: Next you'll use loc and iloc to select specific rows and columns, and boolean conditions to filter a DataFrame down to just the rows you need.

remediation_steps.title: Reading the describe() output
remediation_steps.lede: describe() returns a fixed set of rows. Knowing what each row means lets you read any summary table quickly.

blocks.text: `describe()` computes a set of summary statistics — count, mean, std, min, quartiles (25%, 50%, 75%), and max — for a Series or for each numeric column of a DataFrame in one call. The `50%` row is the median. For the SwiftDrop delivery-time column, `describe()` shows count 7, mean ~30.9, std ~21.9, min 18, 50% (median) 22, and max 80.

before.code:
# Individual calls — one statistic at a time
print(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].mean())    # ~30.9
print(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median())  # 22
print(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].std())     # ~21.9

annotations.text: Three separate calls — each returns one number

after.code:
# describe() — all summary statistics in one call
print(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].describe())
# count     7.0
# mean     ~30.9
# std      ~21.9
# min      18.0
# 25%      21.0
# 50%      22.0   <- median
# 75%      27.0
# max      80.0

annotations.text: describe() returns count, mean, std, min, quartiles, and max
50% row is the median — same as .median()

blocks.change_summary: Three individual stat calls replaced by a single describe() call showing all summary statistics.
